title: Rain slope loss after 1997 was less certain with shared rain support and resampled years in 175 south-east Australian catchments
abstract: We test the reported loss of annual rain sensitivity in 175 south-east Australian catchments. We reuse signed annual CAMELS-AUS tables for 1951-2021. We fit separate current-rain, prior-rain and temperature slopes in each era and resample both reference and later years, plus spatial cells. In 2010-2021 the slope change was -27% for AGCD rain (95% interval -63% to -7%) and -22% for SILO (-38% to +3%). With shared current-rain ranges, these values were -26% (-54% to -4%; 173 catchments) and -17% (-38% to +16%; 168 catchments). In 1997-2009 shared ranges gave -22% for AGCD (-40% to -3%; 102 catchments) and -8% for SILO (-32% to +18%; 92 catchments). On those same 92 gauges, the untrimmed SILO estimate was -26%. Thus rain-range trimming, rather than gauge selection alone, weakens the drought estimate. An exact projection identity separates marginal from partial slope changes. A fixed quadratic synthetic response gives a 10-12% drought slope loss with no parameter change; a correctly specified quadratic fit gives zero. This is a method and evidence audit, not independent data confirmation or physical attribution. Short eras, linear response models, fixed selection and approximate bootstrap limits remain important limits.

display.caption: Rain slope changes with approximate 95 percent limits from synchronous year blocks and spatial cells. Shared-range estimates use smaller fixed cohorts. Current rain, prior rain and temperature have separate coefficients in each era in the full fits.
